title: Care for the whole person
hookLine: Jesuit schools care for the whole person

cards: A report card says a student is failing chemistry. One teacher sees a grade to fix.
Another notices the student has been sleeping in the back row for weeks, asks a quiet question after class, and learns that someone at home is sick and the kid is working nights.

Same student, same grade, two very different pictures of who is sitting in that chair. Jesuit schools have a two-word Latin phrase for the second kind of seeing, and some put it in their mission statements.

teach.h: CURA: CARE. PERSONALIS: OF THE PERSON.
teach.b: Cura personalis. Cura means care; personalis, of the person. In English it usually comes out as care for the whole person.
The idea is older than the slogan.

In the guidance at the start of the Spiritual Exercises, Ignatius keeps telling the director to adapt. Give the Exercises according to the person's age, education and ability. Don't hand anyone more than they can carry.
Notice whether they're in consolation or desolation, and respond to that person, not to a script. The retreat bends to fit the human being, not the other way round.

Later Jesuits, tradition says, used cura personalis for the care superiors owed each member of the order, one by one. Jesuit schools took it up as a promise about students: we aren't only training a mind.

We care about the body that's tired, the heart that's worried, the spirit that's searching. Saint Paul's blessing for the Thessalonians names all three, in the Douay-Rheims: "your whole spirit, and soul, and body."
What makes it more than kindness? A Jesuit classroom is still a classroom, and the chemistry still matters.
Cura personalis doesn't lower the bar; it asks who is trying to clear it, and what they're carrying.

teach.h: YOUR WHOLE SPIRIT, AND SOUL, AND BODY.
teach.b: And it isn't only for schools. A nurse can practice it, a manager, a parent at a kitchen table. It's the difference between how are you, said on the way past, and how are you, said while you stop walking.

how: Jesuit schools and universities describe cura personalis as attention to each student's intellectual, emotional and spiritual life, and the phrase often appears in their mission statements and advising programs.

games.q: you're a teacher. a good student starts failing and sleeping in class. what does cura personalis ask of you first?
o: lower the grade standard for them.
ask quietly what's going on, and listen.
report the grade and move on.
games.why: care for the whole person starts by seeing who's in the chair. the standard can stay; the student is no longer just a grade.

practice: Bring to mind one person you'll see or message soon, a coworker, a parent, a friend who's gone quiet, and picture them not as a role but as a whole person. What might their body be carrying, their mind, their heart?
If you pray, hold that person before God for the length of this sit.

wordCard.voice: Cura personalis. Latin for care of the person: the Jesuit habit of attending to each one as a whole human being, mind, body and spirit. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: care of the person. a phrase Jesuit schools use for their care of each student.

carryVoice: Your line: the whole person. The bar stays where it is, and the care comes with it. Same time tomorrow.
